Tumor microenvironment barriers
The tumor microenvironment (TME) represents a major 
biological barrier to the therapeutic efficacy of g-C₃N₄-
based photocatalytic systems [70]. Although structural 
and surface engineering of g-C₃N₄ can improve light 
absorption, charge separation, and ROS production, the 
therapeutic performance of these nanocatalysts is ulti­
mately determined by their ability to function within the 
chemically heterogeneous and physiologically restrictive 
tumor microenvironment [37]. In particular, elevated 
glutathione (GSH), hypoxia, limited hydrogen peroxide 
(H₂O₂), heterogeneous extracellular acidity, and ineffi­
cient tumor penetration and targeting can substantially 
reduce photocatalytic efficacy.

Although laboratory-scale preparation of g-C₃N₄ nano­
materials is relatively well established, reproducible 
large-scale production remains challenging. Parameters 
such as morphology, particle size distribution, crys­
tallinity, defect density, dopant concentration, surface 
chemistry, and heterostructure composition can strongly 
influence photocatalytic and biological performance [30]. 
Small variations during synthesis may therefore result 
in substantial batch-to-batch differences in therapeutic 
behavior. Standardized synthetic procedures, quality-
control parameters, scalable manufacturing approaches, 
and well-defined structure–property–activity relation­
ships will be essential for future translation.
Biosafety and in vivo validation
Although g-C₃N₄ has shown promising biocompatibil­
ity in several experimental systems, its long-term safety 
profile remains insufficiently established for clinical 
translation. Important considerations include biodistri­

Challenges and future perspectives
Current challenges
Despite substantial progress in the development of 
g-C₃N₄-based nanoplatforms for cancer therapy, several 
physicochemical, biological, and translational challenges 
continue to limit their progression toward clinical 
application.
Limited light penetration
A major limitation of many g-C₃N₄-based photocatalytic 
systems is their dependence on UV–visible or relatively 
short-wavelength light, which has limited penetration 
through biological tissues and may reduce therapeutic 
efficacy in deep-seated tumors. Short-wavelength irra­

surrounding tissues. Consequently, shifting the optical
